newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Countdown begins to new British offshore oil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Countdown begins to new British offshore oil.

text.p: Britain's newest oil province, in deep Atlantic waters off the northern Scottish coast, will come of age next month when first oil flows from the Foinaven field.
Everything is in place for Foinaven to come on stream in April, a spokesman for field operator British Petroleum said this week.
"The exact date is weather-dependent but the only thing that would prevent production in April is something unexpected," he said.

BP will turn on the taps at Foinaven some five years after oil was first discovered in commercial quantities west of the Shetland Islands. Development of the region will stem the decline in British offshore oil output.
"It has the potential to keep the relatively mature UK production scene buoyant well into the next century," said Jason Kenney of Edinburgh-based industry consultants Wood Mackenzie.
But there has been speculation that not only the weather, but action by environmental group Greenpeace could disrupt the start of production at Foinaven.
"There have been rumours that Greenpeace may take action. Whatever they intend, I hope they won't prevent us from going about our lawful and legitimate business," the BP spokesman said.
Nearly two years ago a Greenpeace campaign, including direct action at sea, forced Anglo-Dutch oil giant Shell to abandon plans to ditch its Brent Spar platform in Atlantic waters.
Anyone entering a 500 metre exclusion zone around the Foinaven production vessel without permission would be committing a criminal offence, BP said.
Greenpeace said it was opposed to the development and could not rule out the possibility of future action.
"Opening up pristine ocean for oil development is madness fuelled by greed," said Greenpeace spokesman Matthew Spencer.
Foinaven, which BP discovered in partnership with Shell, should reach peak output of 120,000 barrels per day (bpd) in the second half of this year, BP said.
The field's start up was delayed from last June because of a problem with the subsea infrastructure which will carry crude oil to a floating production and storage vessel.
Crude will be transported by shuttle tanker to the Flotta export terminal on the Orkney islands.

BP and Shell have also made two other commercial finds on the Atlantic margin, Schiehallion, due to start pumping in mid-1998, and Suilven, but more information is still needed to gauge the province's true commercial potential, analysts said.
Britain's offshore oil production should hit a record 2.8 million bpd in 1997, but on the basis of current finds will start to decline early next century, Wood Mackenzie estimates.

Britain's seventeenth offshore licensing round, which closed on Tuesday, will open up 127 new blocks for exploration, mainly in waters southwest of Foinaven-Schiehallion and in the Rockall Trough west of the Hebrides.
"The seventeenth round opens up a whole new frontier area, there could be a lot more potential there that we don't yet know," Kenney said.
Greenpeace has joined 36 oil companies in applying for the blocks.
"Our plans are to do what the government should have done and set aside this 22,000 square miles instead of drilling for oil," said Greenpeace's Spencer.
